# 1 Samuel 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter narrates Saul's first military test as king: the siege of Jabesh-gilead by Nahash the Ammonite, Saul's Spirit-empowered rallying of all Israel, the decisive victory, and the public renewal of Saul's kingship at Gilgal. Commentators across traditions agree this chapter presents Saul "at his best" — humble, Spirit-filled, courageous, merciful, and God-honouring — making his later fall all the more tragic.

**Sources:** EnduringWord.com (Guzik), Gill's Exposition (StudyLight.org), Ellicott's Commentary (StudyLight.org), Precept Austin, Matthew Henry (via BibleHub excerpts), Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (BibleHub).

---

## Verse 1

**v. 1:** *"Soon Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, 'Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.'"*

- **Nahash the Ammonite:** His name means "serpent" in Hebrew. He was king of the Ammonites (1 Sam 12:12), a people descended from Lot (Gen 19:36–38). The Septuagint and Vulgate add "about a month after" Saul's election, a reading also found in Josephus. Gill notes that Nahash had been preparing for war against Israel before this, and now actually marched to besiege Jabesh-gilead, a city in the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Jabesh-gilead's surrender offer:** The men of Jabesh offered to become tributaries (not slaves) to Nahash. Gill remarks that this "showed a mean and abject spirit" — they made no attempt at defence but immediately sought a capitulation, probably because they felt isolated and believed Israel west of the Jordan could not help. Guzik notes Blaikie's lament: "Instead of humbling themselves before God … they put God altogether aside, and basely offered to become the servants of the Ammonites." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Historical context — the Benjamite connection:** Ellicott explains that a deep bond existed between Jabesh-gilead and the tribe of Benjamin. When Israel had nearly annihilated Benjamin (Judges 21), Jabesh-gilead alone refused to join the punitive expedition. The surviving Benjamite warriors were later given the maidens of Jabesh as wives. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Precept Austin** notes that Nahash was a descendant of Lot and that the men of Jabesh were ready to "cut a deal" (the Hebrew *karath beriyth* means "cut a covenant") and become his slaves — an act of spiritual apathy born of godless leadership. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary
- **Text-critical note:** The Dead Sea Scrolls (4QSamᵃ) and Josephus preserve a longer text explaining that Nahash had already been gouging out the right eyes of Israelites east of the Jordan (Gadites and Reubenites), and 7,000 survivors had fled into Jabesh-gilead. The NET Bible notes that this reading "should not be lightly dismissed" but follows the Masoretic text out of caution. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary

---

## Verse 2

**v. 2:** *"But Nahash the Ammonite replied, 'I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone's right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel.'"*

- **The demand to gouge out the right eye:** Gill explains Nahash's dual purpose: (1) to disable the men for war — the left eye was covered by the shield in battle, so removing the right eye made a warrior useless; (2) to bring "reproach upon all Israel," demonstrating that Israel could not protect its own. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Ellicott** calls the demand "horrible cruelty" that "gives us an insight into the barbarous customs of this imperfectly civilised age." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) draws a parallel between Nahash and Satan: "Satan attacks us but cannot do anything against us without our agreement … Satan wants to humiliate us … Satan wants to take away our ability to effectively fight against him … Nahash means serpent or snake." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Precept Austin** notes that Nahash's "cut" — gouging out the eye — was his dark counterpart to the usual animal-cutting that ratified covenants. "Loss of one eye ruins depth perception … Clearly one-eyed warriors would have a high fatality rate!" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary
- **Theodoret** (cited in Clarke, via Guzik): "He who opposes his shield to the enemy with his left hand, thereby hides his left eye, and looks at his enemy with his right eye; he therefore who plucks out that right eye makes men useless in war." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

---

## Verse 3

**v. 3:** *"'Hold off for seven days,' replied the elders of Jabesh, 'and let us send messengers throughout Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.'"*

- **Seven days' respite:** Gill observes this was "as little as could be granted" for messengers to travel and return. Nahash granted it "out of a bravado" — confident Israel was too disunited and Saul too inexperienced to mount a rescue. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **"If there is no one to save us":** Guzik sees in this a picture of the human spiritual condition: "They knew that they must have a savior" — they recognised they could not save themselves. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **The word "deliver"** (Hebrew *yasha'*): Precept Austin notes this is the root from which the name "Jesus" (*Yeshua*) derives, meaning to save, help, or bring into a broad place of safety. It appears prominently in Judges and 1 Samuel where Israel repeatedly needed deliverance. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary
- Ellicott adds that the request was made "in the hope that Saul the Benjamite … would devise some means for their rescue," given the ancient ties between Benjamin and Jabesh. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html

---

## Verse 4

**v. 4:** *"When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and relayed these words in the hearing of the people, they all wept aloud."*

- **Gibeah of Saul:** So called because this was Saul's home city. Gill notes this is the first time Gibeah is designated this way — "he being elected king, it brought an honour to the place." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **The weeping:** Gill explains the people wept "moved with sympathy to their brethren," especially since Benjamin and Jabesh were linked by intermarriage (Judges 21). They also feared the Ammonites would not stop at Jabesh. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Ellicott** notes it was "exactly what might have been expected from Benjamites" — yet "though they grieved so deeply, they do not seem of themselves to have been able to devise any plan for its relief." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Precept Austin** calls the scene a "town hall meeting" that "aroused the emotions of the entire city," with not just sobbing but "great wailing and bemoaning." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary

---

## Verse 5

**v. 5:** *"Just then Saul was returning from the field, behind his oxen. 'What troubles the people?' asked Saul. 'Why are they weeping?' And they relayed to him the words of the men from Jabesh."*

- **Saul still farming:** All commentators note Saul's humility. Though anointed king, he had returned to agricultural work. Gill: "though he was elected king, he was not inaugurated, and did not take upon him any state … he returned to his father's house, and employed himself in rustic affairs." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Ellicott** compares Saul to Gideon (called from the threshing-floor) and to the Roman hero Cincinnatus, who was ploughing when summoned to be dictator — "and to the plough we know that that great man returned when his work was successfully accomplished." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** calls this "the humility of the king of Israel" and sees wisdom in it: "He knew it was the LORD's job to raise him up as king … He didn't have to promote himself or scheme on his own behalf." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** notes Saul "was in no haste to assume regal state. He resumed his country life at Gibeah, waiting till the Lord should call him forth in some emergency." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/11.htm
- **Precept Austin** quotes Cyril Barber: "As if by chance, Saul at this very moment was coming from the fields" — God's sovereign timing arranging the "chess pieces." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary

---

## Verse 6

**v. 6:** *"When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger."*

- **The Spirit of God came upon Saul:** This is described using the Hebrew verb *tsalach* ("rushed upon," "came mightily"). Gill says the Spirit "filled him with pity and compassion … with wisdom and prudence … with fortitude, courage, and resolution." The Targum renders it "the spirit of fortitude from the Lord dwelt on Saul." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Ellicott** explains: "Nothing, perhaps, could have moved Saul so deeply as this news … he was affected not merely by the disgrace to Israel … but by the sore peril which menaced the ancient friend and ally of his tribe. On Saul's heart, thus prepared for action, the Holy Spirit fell, and endued him with extraordinary wisdom, valour, and power." He compares this to the Spirit coming upon Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson — the judges' pattern. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** emphasises the purpose: "It did not come to entertain him or to thrill him. It came to equip him for service … This is always God's pattern." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Righteous anger:** All commentators agree this was not sinful anger. Guzik: "Saul's anger was not out of a personal sense of hurt or offense, but out of a righteous concern for the cause of the LORD among His people." The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics calls it "Divine Indignation" — an anger that is "not sinful (Mark 3:5; Ephesians 4:26)." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/11.htm

### Traditional Distinctives on v. 6:

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (via Guzik/Enduring Word): The Spirit's coming is described in empowerment terms — equipping for service, not for personal thrill. The emphasis is on "doing something for the LORD." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Reformed** (via Ellicott, and John Piper/Desiring God on the broader context): The Spirit's empowerment of Saul is seen within the larger Reformed framework of God's sovereign purposes working even through sinful human choices (the people's sinful demand for a king). Piper notes that God sovereignly works through Israel's evil request to ultimately bring about the Davidic line and Christ. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king
- **Baptist** (via Gill and CH Spurgeon resources at Precept Austin): Gill emphasises that the Spirit imparted "pity, compassion, wisdom, prudence, fortitude, courage, and resolution" — a comprehensive transformation for the task. The sermon "Saul at His Best" (D. Fraser, via BibleHub sermons) highlights that Saul's "self-control, promptitude, courage, capacity, ascription of praise to God, forbearance towards men" were all exhibited here — and that "from such heights he fell," a classic Baptist emphasis on the need for persevering faith. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary

---

## Verse 7

**v. 7:** *"He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers throughout the land of Israel, proclaiming, 'This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.' Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they turned out as one man."*

- **The dismembered oxen as a war-signal:** Gill compares this to the Levite's concubine in Judges 19:29. Ellicott notes that Saul "hewed them in pieces" and "not improbably … cut the oxen into eleven pieces, and sent one to each of the other tribes." Ellicott also cites Ewald's observation that this resembled the Norse "war-arrow" and the Scottish "fire-brand, with both ends dipped in blood." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **"Saul and Samuel":** Guzik notes that Saul's inclusion of Samuel shows he expected the prophet to accompany him into battle, since Saul was responding to the Spirit of God (citing Baldwin). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Gill** adds that Saul named both himself and Samuel because he knew some despised him but would respect Samuel's authority; he also mentions himself first "because of his superior dignity." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **"The fear of the LORD fell on the people":** Gill explains that the people "feared, should they be disobedient, the Lord would cut them to pieces … their minds were impressed with a sense of this affair being of the Lord." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Ellicott** calls it "some such mighty awakening under the influence of the Spirit of the Eternal" and compares it to Psalm 78:65 ("Then the Lord awaked as one out of sleep") and to historic moments when "the peace-loving traders of the marshes of Holland" rose "as one man" to drive out the Spanish armies. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** observes: "When those hunks of ox-flesh came special delivery, all Israel knew there was a leader in Israel who was serious." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

---

## Verse 8

**v. 8:** *"And when Saul numbered them at Bezek, there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah."*

- **Bezek:** Ellicott locates it in the tribe of Issachar, in the plain of Jezreel — "an open district, well adapted for the assembling of the great host." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **The numbers and Judah's small contingent:** Ellicott suggests the separate mention of Judah and its disproportionately small number reflects the reality that "Judah always stood apart until there was a king who belonged to itself." Judah only began taking an active interest in national welfare under David. He also cautions that "in the Old Testament Books, owing to the mistakes of copyists, numbers are not always to be strictly relied upon." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** notes Josephus gave figures of 700,000 Israelites and 70,000 of Judah — "a gross mistake … contrary to the text." The Septuagint has 600,000 and 70,000. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** also notes an alternative rendering: some take "Bezek" not as a place name but as meaning "with a stone" or "with a fragment" — i.e., the method of counting by collecting stones or broken pieces. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html

---

## Verse 9

**v. 9:** *"So they said to the messengers who had come, 'Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: "Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot."' And when the messengers relayed this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced."*

- **"By the time the sun is hot":** Ellicott explains this means about noon. The distance from Bezek to Jabesh was "not much over twenty miles." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** notes that Josephus says the assistance was promised on the third day (not the next day), because the "morrow" was reckoned from the messengers' return home, not from the day they departed from Saul. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **"And they were glad":** Guzik draws the spiritual application: "Before they did not know if there was anyone to save them. Now they knew they had someone to save them. Knowing we have a savior should make us glad." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

---

## Verse 10

**v. 10:** *"Then the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, 'Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.'"*

- **The deception:** Gill calls this "an artifice" — the men of Jabesh gave the impression of surrender, making the Ammonites "secure, and not at all upon their guard against an approaching enemy." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** (citing Baldwin): "The message contained a clever ambiguity, while giving the impression that surrender was intended." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

---

## Verse 11

**v. 11:** *"The next day Saul organized the troops into three divisions, and during the morning watch they invaded the camp of the Ammonites and slaughtered them, until the hottest part of the day. And the survivors were so scattered that no two of them were left together."*

- **Three companies:** Gill observes that dividing into three was "their way of fighting in those days," citing Gideon (Judges 7:16) and Abimelech (Judges 9:43). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **The morning watch:** Ellicott explains this was "the last of the three watches, each lasting for four hours … the old Hebrew division of the night," meaning the attack came between 2 and 6 a.m. The battle and rout continued "for many hours." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Speed of the march:** Gill computes the distance from Gibeah to Bezek at about 40 miles, and from Bezek to Jabesh another 16 miles — "so quick was Saul and his men in their march, though on foot." Josephus says it was ten *schaeni* (50–60 miles). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Total victory:** Gill notes that those who survived "were scattered … so that two of them were not left together" — "every one shifted for himself, and fled alone." Josephus adds that Nahash himself was slain. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The defeat was "sudden, unexpected, and complete." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/11.htm

---

## Verse 12

**v. 12:** *"Then the people said to Samuel, 'Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!'"*

- **The people turn to Samuel:** Ellicott observes that even "in the first flush of this great victory of Saul's," the people addressed Samuel — showing "the great weight and influence of the seer among the people." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **The reference to the dissenters:** The people refer to the "sons of Belial" who had questioned Saul's fitness in 1 Samuel 10:27. Gill notes the people were now "transported … with affection to Saul, and indignation against those men." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** also notes that Samuel's presence here suggests he either accompanied Saul on the rapid march or "followed after him gently" and met them after the battle. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html

---

## Verse 13

**v. 13:** *"But Saul ordered, 'No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.'"*

- **Saul's magnanimity:** Ellicott calls this "a wise, as well as a generous, decision" — bloody vengeance would have sparked "future feuds and bitter heart-burnings." Saul taught "kings to be" that forgiveness of wrongs was a "truly royal virtue." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** notes Saul "prevented Samuel from giving an answer, being ready to forgive injuries." He adds that "it plainly appears that this temper did not always continue with him." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Guzik** highlights the spiritual dimension: "Satan, having failed in the attack through Nahash, now tried to attack Israel — even in victory — by dividing the nation against each other." Saul wisely resisted this temptation. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Ascription of praise to God:** Saul did not claim credit. Gill: "He does not ascribe the victory to the quick dispatch he made, to his wisdom and prudence … but to the power and goodness of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** reflects: "Nothing could be better than his *Te Deum laudamus* — 'Today Jehovah hath wrought salvation in Israel.'" — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/11.htm
- **Saul's refusal as a pattern of divine clemency:** Ellicott quotes Seb. Schmidt (via Keil & Delitzsch): Saul "reminded them of the clemency of God, and urged that since Jehovah had shown such clemency upon that day … it was only right they should follow His example, and forgive their neighbours' sins without bloodshed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html

### Traditional Distinctives on v. 13:

- **Reformed** (via John Piper/Desiring God): Piper ties this chapter to 1 Samuel 12, where Samuel makes clear that Israel's demand for a king was "a great evil" — they were rejecting God as king. Yet "the sovereign purposes of God … are not frustrated, but are fulfilled even by the sins of his people." Saul's salvation here is a picture of God working good through flawed human instruments. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-evil-origin-of-a-good-king
- **Baptist** (via Gill and Spurgeon circles): The sermon "Saul at His Best" (D. Fraser, via Precept Austin) notes Saul's "ascription of praise to God" and "forbearance towards men" as virtues — yet the warning is stark: "from this moral elevation Saul miserably fell … He who showed at first patience and self-control became a restless, jealous king." This fits the Baptist emphasis on the necessity of persevering grace. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-11-commentary

---

## Verse 14

**v. 14:** *"Then Samuel said to the people, 'Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.'"*

- **Samuel's strategic wisdom:** Guzik notes that Samuel "wisely sees this time of victory as a strategic opportunity to renew the kingdom" since many had not fully accepted Saul at Mizpeh (1 Sam 10:27). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **Ellicott** highlights Samuel's "striking generosity to one who superseded him in his position as judge" — Samuel again presented Saul to Israel as their king. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gilgal:** Ellicott describes it as "the well-known sanctuary" situated "in the Jordan Valley, not far from Jericho," in the tribe of Benjamin, and "the scene of many of the most striking events in Israelitic history." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Gill** adds that Gilgal was "the nearest place to them, on the other side Jordan," where Israel first encamped after crossing the Jordan, where the tabernacle and ark had been, and where an altar was built. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html

---

## Verse 15

**v. 15:** *"So all the people went to Gilgal and confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly."*

- **"They made Saul king before the LORD":** Gill clarifies this was a public declaration and investiture: "otherwise it was God only that made him king, who only had the power of making one, see Acts 2:36." Josephus and the Septuagint say Samuel anointed Saul with oil at this time, and Gill thinks it not improbable — though Ellicott disagrees, stating "the Gilgal convention was nothing more than a solemn national confirmation of the popular election at Mizpeh," not a re-anointing. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **"Before the LORD":** Ellicott says this implies the presence of the Ark or the high priest with the Urim and Thummim. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Peace offerings:** Gill explains these were "by way of thanksgiving, partly for the victory obtained over the Ammonites, and partly for the renewal of the kingdom to Saul, and their unanimity in it, as well as to implore and obtain future peace and prosperity." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Rejoicing:** Guzik notes "they felt they had a king, and a good king. It is a great blessing to be under a great, victorious king." He then applies it to Christ: "Jesus is our King. The Father hath anointed Him … but sometimes our sense of loyalty and devotion wanes … therefore we need, from time to time, to renew the kingdom" (quoting F.B. Meyer). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/
- **The tragic foreshadowing:** Guzik closes with Blaikie's lament: "O Saul, Saul, how well for thee it would have been hadst thou maintained this spirit! For then God would not have had to reject thee from being king." Saul's greatest victories in this chapter were "not only military but inward — defeating pride, insecurity, and the desire for revenge." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

### Traditional Distinctives on vv. 14–15:

- **Anglican** (via Ellicott): The emphasis on Gilgal as a "well-known sanctuary," the "presence of the Ark," and the "solemn national confirmation" reflects an Anglican sensitivity to liturgical and sacramental space — sacred geography and ritual confirmation matter. Ellicott also quotes Bishop Wordsworth's view that the people "made him to assume the royal state and authority." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-11.html
- **Baptist** (via Gill): The emphasis is on God alone making Saul king (citing Acts 2:36 — God made Jesus both Lord and Christ), with the human ceremony being a declaration, not the source of authority. The peace offerings are "thanksgiving" — not meritorious but responsive. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-11.html
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (via Guzik/Enduring Word): The application moves quickly from the historical event to the personal devotional — "Jesus is our King … we need, from time to time, to renew the kingdom." The emphasis is on the believer's experiential renewal of devotion. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-11/

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Shared Emphasis | Distinctive Nuance |
|---|---|---|
| **The Spirit's empowering** (v. 6) | All agree it was for service, not self | Pentecostal: practical empowerment language; Reformed: placed in God's sovereign redemptive plan |
| **Righteous anger** (v. 6) | Not sinful; Spirit-led concern for God's honour | Universal agreement across traditions |
| **Saul's humility** (v. 5) | All commend his return to farm work | Baptist/Gill: notes "rustic affairs" as proper; Anglican/Ellicott: classical comparison to Cincinnatus |
| **Saul's mercy** (vv. 12–13) | All praise it as wise and godly | Reformed/Piper: part of God's larger redemptive story despite Israel's sin; Baptist: a warning that this virtue did not last |
| **The Gilgal ceremony** (vv. 14–15) | Public confirmation of kingship | Anglican: emphasis on sanctuary, ritual, presence of Ark; Baptist: God alone makes kings — the ceremony declares, not creates |
| **Nahash as type of Satan** (vv. 1–2) | Guzik develops this fully; traditional commentators note the name "serpent" | Pentecostal/Charismatic: explicit spiritual-warfare typology; older commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Henry): more restrained, historical focus |
